config.title: Build graceful shutdown with in flight drain

intro.title: Build graceful shutdown with in flight drain
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a Node.js server that gracefully shuts down, ensuring it completes any ongoing requests before stopping. You will learn the core concept of handling in-flight requests, which are requests that have been received but not yet fully processed. The main technologies involved are the Node.js HTTP module for creating a server and the process object for listening to shutdown signals. You'll implement a mechanism to track active requests and drain them safely, preventing abrupt interruptions. This practice is essential for building reliable, production-ready applications that maintain data integrity and user experience.
intro.usecase: Graceful shutdown with in-flight request draining is a critical pattern for any production Node.js server handling user traffic, such as a web application dashboard or an API backend. When deploying updates or scaling down, this pattern ensures that users completing actions—like submitting a form, processing a payment, or loading data in a panel—do not experience errors or data loss. For example, an e-commerce checkout flow or a real-time analytics dashboard must finish processing ongoing requests before the server stops to maintain reliability and a positive user experience. Implementing this allows developers to perform zero-downtime deployments and maintain service integrity during maintenance.

objectives: Implement a signal handler to capture shutdown signals in a Node.js server
Configure server settings to reject new connections during graceful shutdown
Initialize a tracking mechanism to monitor in-flight requests
Construct a request drain function that waits for active requests to complete
Integrate the drain function with the server's close method
Manipulate server state to transition from active to draining to stopped
Apply timeout controls to prevent indefinite shutdown hangs

steps.title: Import required Node.js modules
steps.instruction: Import the http module for creating a server and the process object for handling shutdown signals.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import Node.js core modules. The http module is built into Node.js, and process is a global object.
steps.seedCode: // Import the http module and the process object here
steps.expectedOutcome: The http module and process object are imported and ready to use for server creation and signal handling.
successCriteria: The http module is imported using require('http'), and the process object is accessible globally.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're importing the http module using require('http'). The process object is global, so no explicit import is needed.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import syntax. Use require('http') to import the http module. Remember that process is a global object in Node.js.

steps.title: Create a basic HTTP server
steps.instruction: Create an HTTP server using http.createServer() that returns a simple 'Hello, world!' response with status code 200.
steps.hint: Use the http.createServer() method and pass it a callback function that handles requests and responses. Inside the callback, set the response status code to 200 and end the response with 'Hello, world!'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A server variable is created that listens for HTTP requests and responds with 'Hello, world!'.
successCriteria: The server is created using http.createServer() and responds with status 200 and 'Hello, world!'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your server responds with status 200 and 'Hello, world!'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using http.createServer() correctly and ending the response with 'Hello, world!'.

steps.title: Add server listening on a port
steps.instruction: Call the server's listen method on port 3000 and log a message when the server starts.
steps.hint: Use server.listen(3000, () => { console.log(...) }) to start the server and log a startup message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will start listening on port 3000 and log 'Server running on port 3000' to the console.
successCriteria: A callback logs a startup message
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you call server.listen with port 3000 and include a callback that logs a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: server.listen(port, callback) where the callback logs a startup message.

steps.title: Initialize variables for tracking in-flight requests
steps.instruction: Right after creating the server, declare two variables: 1) A Set named 'activeConnections' to track ongoing requests, and 2) A boolean named 'isShuttingDown' initialized to false.
steps.hint: Use 'const' for the Set and 'let' for the boolean flag. Place them after the server creation but before the server.listen call.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a Set to monitor active connections and a boolean flag to indicate shutdown state, ready for graceful shutdown logic.
successCriteria: Variables 'activeConnections' (a Set) and 'isShuttingDown' (boolean false) are declared after server creation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you declared both variables: a Set named 'activeConnections' and a boolean 'isShuttingDown' set to false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction: you need to declare two variables after creating the server. One should be a Set, the other a boolean flag.

steps.title: Modify server to track active connections
steps.instruction: Inside the server's request handler, add the current request's socket to the 'connections' Set when a request starts, and remove it when the response finishes.
steps.hint: Access the request's socket with req.socket. Add it to the Set with connections.add(). Remove it in the response's 'close' event listener.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now track each active connection in the 'connections' Set, adding when requests start and removing when responses complete.
successCriteria: The request handler adds req.socket to connections and sets up removal in the response's 'close' event
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're adding req.socket to connections and removing it when the response finishes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The connection tracking isn't complete. Remember to add the socket when the request starts and remove it when the response ends.

steps.title: Create graceful shutdown handler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named gracefulShutdown that sets a shutdown flag, stops the server from accepting new connections, and begins draining existing connections.
steps.hint: Define a function that logs a shutdown message, sets a boolean flag, calls server.close() to stop new connections, and then handles draining.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named gracefulShutdown is defined that logs a message, sets a shutdown flag, and calls server.close().
successCriteria: The gracefulShutdown function is defined, logs a shutdown message, sets a boolean flag, and calls server.close().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the shutdown function, but make sure it logs a message, sets a shutdown flag, and calls server.close() to stop new connections.
steps.feedbackWrong: The graceful shutdown function is not correctly defined. It should be named gracefulShutdown, log a message, set a flag, and call server.close().

steps.title: Add signal handlers for shutdown triggers
steps.instruction: Add two event listeners using process.on() to handle SIGTERM and SIGINT signals, both calling the shutdown function.
steps.hint: Use process.on('SIGTERM', shutdown) and process.on('SIGINT', shutdown) to listen for shutdown signals.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now respond to termination signals by calling the shutdown function.
successCriteria: process.on listeners for SIGTERM and SIGINT are added, both calling the shutdown function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added at least one signal handler, but make sure to handle both SIGTERM and SIGINT signals.
steps.feedbackWrong: The signal handlers are missing or not properly configured. Add process.on() listeners for both SIGTERM and SIGINT that call the shutdown function.

steps.title: Implement in-flight request draining logic
steps.instruction: Inside your graceful shutdown handler function, add a setInterval that periodically checks if the active connections Set is empty, and when empty, clears the interval and calls process.exit(0).
steps.hint: Use setInterval to create a loop that checks connections.size. When it's 0, clear the interval with clearInterval and exit.
steps.expectedOutcome: The shutdown handler will now actively monitor and wait for all in-flight requests to complete before exiting.
successCriteria: The graceful shutdown handler contains a setInterval that checks connections.size and exits when empty.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your setInterval checks connections.size and calls process.exit(0) when it's 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: The draining logic isn't quite right. The shutdown handler needs to periodically check if connections are empty before exiting.

steps.title: Test the graceful shutdown implementation
steps.instruction: Run the server using `node server.js` in your terminal, send multiple HTTP requests to http://localhost:3000,
steps.hint: Open multiple browser tabs or use curl commands to send requests while the server is running, then interrupt the process to see the graceful shutdown in action.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see the server start, handle incoming requests, then when you press Ctrl+C, it should log shutdown messages, wait for in-flight requests to complete, and finally exit cleanly.
successCriteria: Server runs successfully, handles requests, and performs graceful shutdown with visible draining behavior when interrupted.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: The server runs but the shutdown behavior might not be fully visible. Make sure you send multiple requests while the server is running before triggering shutdown.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't running or the shutdown isn't working as expected. Check that all previous steps are correctly implemented and the server starts properly.
